newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Marcos victims in Philippines welcome U.S. verdict.
newsitem.headline: Marcos victims in Philippines welcome U.S. verdict.

text.p: Lawyers and human rights activists in the Philippines on Wednesday welcomed a U.S. court verdict upholding a $1.9 billion award for victims of former strongman Ferdinand Marcos but said more legal battles could be in the offing.

The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled on Tuesday that former Philippine president Marcos, who died in exile in 1989, could be held liable for abuses while in power and affirmed the compensation awarded by a court in Honolulu in 1994 to the estimated 9,500 victims.
Former first lady Imelda Marcos withheld immediate comment but an aide said her lawyers had told her of the ruling.
The aide said the lawyers had not decided on the next move but "the next logical step would be to go to the U.S. Supreme Court".
"A just verdict that even time cannot erase," Rod Domingo, a lawyer for the victims, said in a statement.
"Oppressors of human rights the world over are now warned they cannot get away with their inhumanities to mankind."
Leftist leader Satur Ocampo, one of the claimants, called Tuesday's ruling a moral and political victory for the victims.
He said the Manila government, which has also staked a claim to the Marcos fortune, had a moral obligation to ensure the claimants were compensated.
"In the interest of the goverment's campaign towards national reconciliation, this is a requisite in order to close a dark chapter in the history of our country," Ocampo said.
But Ocampo acknowledged it was possible it would take several more years before the victims could benefit from the award.
The Manila government has accused the Marcoses and their business associates of stealing up to $5 billion from the economy during Marcos's 20-year rule and says it has priority claim over the assets.

"I am happy for the victims...but at some point in time there might be a conflict between them and the government," said Magtanggol Gunigundo, chairman of a state commission pursuing the Marcos assets. "I think we may be able to reach a compromise.
"But with more claimants surfacing, the situation is becoming more complicated," he said.
